slides.title: Learning outcomes, Program Outcomes, Assignments and Authentic assessment
text: Learning outcomes, Program Outcomes, Assignments and Authentic assessment
notes: The professional practices course was developed to address difficulties with soft topic coverage in the degree plan used for many years, along with increased needs that arose from broadening the available degree programs and heightened expectations for computing curricula. Throughout the 80's and 90's, the CSE department offered a single undergraduate degree in Computer Science and Engineering. The first year of the program included a one-hour college-level common course (1104) Introduction to Engineering to provide exposure to the diversity of challenges in engineering, along with another one-hour departmental course (1105) Introduction to Computer Science and Engineering to address further topics on responsibilities and expectations for students in computing. The two-semester capstone senior design sequence (4316/4317) emphasizes an extended design experience in a team setting, but had the additional responsibility for delivering substantial knowledge and assessing student achievement on nontechnical student outcomes. This situation often led to uneven coverage of the non-technical topics from semester to semester depending upon the instructor. Students also found it very challenging to balance between learning the technical topics and soft topics simultaneously. The topics covered in the professional practices course provide a just-in-time coverage of the topics most needed at this stage, and was the primary motivation for offering this class. The new course was also needed to strengthen compliance with ABET criteria as discussed below. In 2003, additional programs in Computer Science and Software Engineering were accredited through CAC and EAC, respectively. After a re-accreditation visit for all three programs in 2006, the Computer Science and Engineering program was renamed to Computer Engineering. Like all ABET accredited programs, each of the three programs has a list of educational objectives (PEOs). These can be found on the departmental website http://cse.uta.edu/ but may be summarized as follows: 1. Initial employment 2. Advance in responsibilities 3. Demonstrate leadership The PEOs are mapped to student learning outcomes and the three degree plans in the following systematic fashion. PEO 1 regards fundamentals indispensable in any effort involving computing in the few years following graduation. PEO 2 regards broader design and teamwork responsibilities. PEO 3 includes attitudes, values, and altruism as a seasoned computing professional of the broadest perspective. When viewed this way, PEO 3 involves the following EAC and CAC student outcomes.
What characteristics should a professional exhibit?

Professional bodies each have their own ideas of the characteristics that their members should possess to be considered "a professional". These are stated in their codes of conduct and ethics and all of the bodies have their own versions of these. Certain items appear in all of them including:
keeping up to date with the field
helping their colleagues advance within their field
showing concern for the well being of their clients
adhering to the relevant legislation
respecting client confidentiality
we can see that a professional:
is engaged in one of the learned professions
has a calling requiring specialized knowledge and often long and intensive academic preparation
is characterized by or conforming to the technical or ethical standards of a profession
So professionals spend a long time studying a particular calling

slides.title: Feedback Assignment 1:
text: Feedback Assignment 1:
Writing & Referencing — Critical Weakness (59.3% avg)
This is the weakest area across all students. Students averaged 5.93/10 marks, indicating widespread struggles with academic integrity and professional communication.
Missing In-Text Citations: Most students fail to provide proper APA citations for claims, statistics, and evidence. This is repeatedly mentioned as the primary reason for lost marks.
APA Format Inconsistencies: Even when citations are attempted, errors in APA 7th edition formatting are common—incorrect author-year format, missing page numbers, improper reference lists.
Grammatical & Typographical Errors: Many submissions contain spelling mistakes, grammatical errors, and inconsistent formatting.
Weak Transitions: Students struggle with creating seamless transitions between ideas and sections, resulting in arguments that are disjointed.

slides.title: Feedback Assignment 1:
text: Feedback Assignment 1:
2. Problem Statement — Critical Analysis (69.5% avg)
Students show basic understanding but lack depth in critical thinking. Average score of 17.37/25 indicates significant room for improvement.
Shallow HOW Analysis: Descriptions of how AI should work are superficial, lacking technical depth in algorithmic mechanisms and implementation details.
Weak WHAT Definition: Ethical problems are identified but with limited theoretical application—students fail to clearly define the nature and scope using ethical frameworks.
Missing Root Cause Analysis: Basic understanding of causation without identifying root causes, cascading effects, or underlying reasons why ethical issues emerge.
Limited Perspectives: Insufficient consideration of multiple stakeholder perspectives—arguments lack substantial evidence

slides.title: Feedback Assignment 1:
text: Feedback Assignment 1:
3. Literature Review — Source Analysis (69.7% avg)
Analysis tends to be descriptive rather than critical. Students averaged 17.42/25 marks.
Descriptive vs. Analytical: Students often describe case studies and sources rather than conducting a systematic analysis of how technical limitations create ethical vulnerabilities.
Poor Source Integration: Instead of synthesizing multiple perspectives to build a nuanced understanding, students present separate narratives from different sources.
Superficial Technical Understanding: Limited depth in explaining AI techniques and their operational mechanisms—many show only basic understanding.
Insufficient Critical Evaluation: Students do not critically evaluate sources or establish clear connections between technical functionality and ethical outcomes.

slides.title: Feedback Assignment 1:
text: Feedback Assignment 1:
4. Conclusion — Synthesis (70.5% avg)
Relatively strong area but still room for improvement. Students averaged 14.10/20 marks.
Incomplete Synthesis: While students summarize findings adequately, they do not create comprehensive synthesis that weaves together all investigation elements.
Lack of Forward-Looking Insights: Missing reflection on emerging trends, future implications, or specific recommendations for professional development.
Limited Broader Impact: Insufficient critical reflection on implications for the broader computing field beyond immediate case study findings.

slides.title: Feedback Assignment 1:
text: Feedback Assignment 1:
5. Introduction — Context & Significance (71.7% avg)
Strongest area overall. Students averaged 14.34/20 marks, but improvement still possible.
Lack of Quantitative Evidence: Introductions often lack specific statistics, numerical data, or metrics to demonstrate severity and impact.
Weak Topic Justification: Students fail to provide compelling, evidence-based arguments for topic significance using multiple authoritative sources.
Missing Professional Relevance: Insufficient explanation of why computing professionals must engage with the ethical issue.

slides.title: In summary main Cognitive Skills to develop is Cognitive (Analysis)
text: In summary main Cognitive Skills to develop is Cognitive (Analysis)
Developing this Cognitive Analysis skills involve:
Examining content: Identifying main ideas, supporting evidence, and key arguments within research materials.
Recognizing structure: Understanding how information is organized, identifying patterns, relationships, and organizational principles.
Identifying relationships: Seeing connections between concepts, detecting cause-and-effect relationships, and recognizing how different elements work together.
Distinguishing components: Breaking down complex ideas into manageable parts to better understand the whole.
notes: Identify and analyse complex computing problems reaching substantiated conclusions using fundamental principles of mathematics, computing and data sciences, and relevant domain knowledge

How to Apply Analysis in Research Assignments (which is provided by marking rubric criterion to guide you in this skill development):

Break down scholarly articles to understand their methodology, findings, and conclusions

Identify underlying assumptions in arguments
Recognize patterns across multiple sources

How is this a skill for lifelong learning?
Self-Directed Learning: Strong analysis skills empower individuals to:
Identify knowledge gaps: Recognizing what you know and what you need to learn
Evaluate learning resources: Determining which sources are most valuable for your needs
Structure personal learning: Creating effective self-study approaches tailored to your goals
Monitor understanding: Assessing your grasp of new information and adjusting as needed
